metadata.title: Matrix Transformation: Columns Are Where the Basis Vectors Land
metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.objective: Show how a matrix maps basis vectors and a shape in the plane.
metadata.learner: Has seen vectors but not matrix geometry.
misconceptions: Matrix multiplication is just elementwise multiplication
expectedUnderstanding: The first column of M is the image of e1 and the second column is the image of e2.
Every point, and therefore every edge of the unit square, is sent to M times that point.
The whole grid is carried along, so vertical lines tilt and horizontal lines stretch by the entry a.

primitives.text: A matrix moves the basis vectors, the grid, and every shape together
M = [ [a, b], [0, 1] ]   the columns are where e1 and e2 land
Grey outline: the original unit square. Drag a and b and watch the grid follow.
det M = a*1 - b*0 = a, so areas scale by |a| and the shape flattens when a = 0

controls.label: Change entry a: stretch of the first column
Change entry b: tilt of the second column

checkpoints.title: Read the columns
checkpoints.body: The grey square is the original unit square, spanned by e1 and e2. The matrix M has first column (a, 0) and second column (b, 1): those are exactly where the two basis vectors land.

checkpoints.title: The shape follows the corners
checkpoints.body: Each corner p is sent to M p. So (0,0), (1,0), (1,1), (0,1) become (0,0), (a,0), (a+b,1), (b,1). The blue parallelogram is the unit square after the map.

checkpoints.title: The grid itself moves
checkpoints.body: The whole grid is carried along: former vertical lines tilt by b, former horizontal lines stretch by a. A transformed grid is visibly different, so the transformation is not elementwise multiplication of the entries.

checkpoints.title: Area and determinant
checkpoints.body: det M = a*1 - b*0 = a, so the area of the image of the unit square is |a|. Push a toward 0 and the shape collapses onto a line; make a negative and it flips to the other side.

narration.text: Here is the plane with a unit square. The matrix M will move everything in it.
Its first column is a zero: that is where the first basis vector goes. The second column, b one, is where the second basis vector goes.
Notice the grid is not left alone. Vertical lines tilt, horizontal lines stretch, and every corner moves by the same rule.
The determinant of this matrix is a, so the square's area scales by the size of a. At a equal to zero the square is squashed flat.

fallback.text: Static figure. A light grid of vertical and horizontal lines in the plane, with a grey unit square at the origin. The matrix M = [[a,b],[0,1]] sends the basis vector e1 to (a,0), drawn as an arrow along the horizontal axis, and e2 to (b,1), drawn as a tilted arrow. The unit square becomes the blue parallelogram with corners (0,0), (a,0), (a+b,1), (b,1). Vertical grid lines tilt and horizontal grid lines stretch, so the grid visibly changes. The determinant is a, so areas scale by |a|.

accessibility.alt: A plane with a unit square at the origin and a grid. Arrows show the basis vectors sent to the matrix columns: e1 to (a,0) and e2 to (b,1), tilted upward. The square becomes a parallelogram with the same moved corners, and the grid lines tilt and stretch with it. Areas scale by the determinant a.
